strengths: Well-motivated problem: 30% of UltraFeedback samples show conflicts between fine-grained and holistic preferences, clearly demonstrating the practical relevance of the work
Solid theoretical framework: DMPO objective properly derived from multi-preference PPO, with rigorous loss bounds (Theorems 3.6-3.7) and detailed proofs
Effective theory-practice bridge: Cross-pseudo reward approximation and length bias mitigation (balanced sampling + explicit penalty) are well-designed and implementable
Comprehensive empirical evaluation: Multiple test sets, evaluation metrics, conflict levels, reasonable baselines, and good ablation studies showing design choices matter
Strong empirical results: 10%+ relative improvement vs. both holistic and oracle baselines while using only 30% of data and improving training efficiency
Reproducibility: Detailed implementation, hyperparameters, algorithm description, and supplementary analyses enable reproduction
weaknesses: Limited evaluation scope: Only UltraFeedback dataset tested; conflicts are artificially created via sampling weights rather than naturally-occurring, limiting real-world applicability claims

Unvalidated theoretical assumptions: Theorem 3.7's 'mild condition' 2(κ-1)r/κ ≤ c₂-c₀ is not empirically verified; Definition 3.2's strict ordering assumption is idealistic; bounds depend on unknown constants that may be loose

Ad-hoc PD estimation design: Quantile normalization choices (γ, etc.) lack justification; method requires training K reward models on 30% of data; Figure B.3 shows non-zero prediction conflicts suggesting imperfect estimation
Missing critical sensitivity analyses: No ablation on hyperparameters (τ, γ, ρ); no study of sensitivity to number of sub-preferences; limited budget range analysis; no failure mode discussion
Incomplete length bias mitigation evidence: Simple linear penalty strategies employed; unclear if OURS fully eliminates length bias; Table 2 shows modest length differences vs. baselines
Narrow experimental scope limits generalization: Only Llama 3.1-8B/3.2-3B tested; no comparison with other multi-preference alignment methods (e.g., Zhou et al. 2024); oracle baseline unrealistic
Theory-practice gap: Unclear when theoretical conditions hold in practice; empirical validation of assumption validity is missing; connection between DMPO bounds and actual performance unexplored

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clear identification of practical challenge with 28.6% preference conflicts in UltraFeedback
Rigorous theoretical framework: DMPO derived from first principles with formal loss bounds (Theorems 3.6-3.7)
Clear and intuitive methodology: Selecting high-consensus data (negative PD values) is easy to understand and implement
Thoughtful implementation: Length bias mitigation and PD estimation strategies are well-designed
Comprehensive supplementary analysis: Extensive ablations, budget sensitivity studies, and reward model conflict analysis
weaknesses: Critical experimental limitation: All experiments use artificially constructed conflicts on a single dataset (UltraFeedback); no evaluation on naturally occurring fine-grained preference data undermines practical applicability claims

Significant theory-practice gap: Theory assumes known φₖ values but practice requires estimation via proxy models; approximation error impact unanalyzed. Theorem 3.7 conditions never empirically verified.

Reward model quality not thoroughly investigated: Figure B.3 shows 8-18% prediction conflict; propagation to final performance unexplored. Missing ablations on quantile parameter γ and balance temperature τ

Limited baseline comparisons: No comparison to recent data selection methods (Deng et al. 2025, Lee et al. 2025, Gao et al. 2025). Oracle baseline is artificial. DMPO on full data sometimes underperforms.
Narrow experimental scope: Only Llama-3.1-8B (single size), no evaluation on multiple architectures. Fixed selection budget (30%). No analysis of method with >4 aspects or varying aspect importance
Incremental novelty: DMPO is straightforward DPO extension; PD-based selection is natural consequence rather than surprising insight
Length bias claims not fully substantiated: No conclusive evidence that proposed mitigation eliminates bias; length penalty coefficient ρ lacks principled guidance
Reproducibility concerns: No code release mentioned; hyperparameters (ρ, γ, τ) underspecified; dataset conflict construction procedure could be clearer

strengths: Well-motivated problem with compelling evidence (30% conflicts in UltraFeedback) for why fine-grained preferences are needed but introduce challenges
Solid theoretical contributions: sound DMPO derivation, rigorous loss bound analysis (Theorems 3.6-3.7), and elegant exchange argument proving optimality of high-consensus selection
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple metrics (AlpacaEval 2, length-controlled scores, pairwise evaluation on 5 datasets) and systematically controlled conflict levels
Strong and consistent empirical results: >10% relative improvement over oracle baseline while using only 30% of training data, across all conflict levels
Thoughtful practical implementation with clever cross-pseudo reward estimation for PD term and explicit length bias mitigation through both sampling strategy and loss penalty
Clear presentation with good intuitive explanations of the PD term's role as implicit sample weighting mechanism
Enables a new practical paradigm where fine-grained preference collection + data selection replaces infeasible holistic annotation
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: theorem assumes known φk but practice requires error-prone pseudo-reward estimation; effects of estimation errors on loss bounds not analyzed
Theorem 3.7's 'mild condition' (2(κ-1)/κ·r ≤ c2-c0) not verified empirically; restrictiveness and practical implications unclear
Limited experimental scope: evaluation only on UltraFeedback variants with fixed 4 aspects; lacks validation on diverse datasets with different aspect counts or types

PD estimation uses non-standard 'all-in-one' model with system prompts trained on 30% of data; design choice not well justified compared to separate reward models; quantile normalization removes theoretical interpretability
Core selection principle (prioritizing high-consensus samples) is relatively intuitive once PD term identified; novelty somewhat incremental over identifying the PD term itself
Incomplete baseline comparisons: missing recent data selection methods for preference optimization; Oracle baseline requiring 4x annotation effort is somewhat unrealistic
Computational overhead substantial (52.2 GPU hours total vs 33.6 for baseline); scalability concerns for scenarios with many aspects (κ >> 4)
Notation and definitions could be clearer: c0, c1, c2 introduced without clear motivation; Definition 3.3 assumes non-existent ground-truth holistic reward
